title: The Holy Spirit (CCC 683–690)
hookLine: the advocate and comforter, the breath of the Church

cards: Picture a courtroom. You're on trial, and you don't speak the language. Everyone talks fast, the papers make no sense, and you're completely alone.
Then someone walks in, sits down beside you, puts a hand on your shoulder, and says: I'm with you. I'll speak for you.
The night before he died, Jesus promised his friends someone exactly like that, using a Greek word from the courtroom.
And after he rose, he gave that someone to them in the most intimate way imaginable: with his own breath.

teach.b: At the Last Supper, in John's Gospel, Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "And I will ask the Father, and he shall give you another Paraclete, that he may abide with you for ever."
Paraclete is the Greek parakletos: someone called to your side. In a law court, an advocate. In grief, a comforter.
English Bibles have tried both words, and neither holds all of it. Notice the word another. Jesus has been their Paraclete; now a second one is coming, who won't leave.
Then the breath. On Easter evening the disciples are behind locked doors, afraid.

Jesus stands among them, and John says "he breathed on them; and he said to them: Receive ye the Holy Ghost." In both Hebrew and Greek, the word for spirit is also the word for breath and wind: ruach, pneuma.
The Bible's first breath is God breathing life into the first human. Here the risen Jesus breathes again, and a new creation starts. How is the Spirit known?
The Catechism says the Spirit is the one who lets anyone say Jesus is Lord at all, and yet he doesn't speak of himself.
Catholics say they know him by what he does: in the Scriptures he inspired, in the sacraments, in prayer, in the gifts given to ordinary believers, and in the lives of the saints.

teach.h: THE SON AND THE SPIRIT, SENT TOGETHER.
teach.b: And the Son and the Spirit, the Catechism says, are always sent together; you don't get one without the other.
Catholics say the Spirit is the reason the Church is alive at all, the way breath is the reason a body is.

how: Catholics call on the Holy Spirit with the prayer that begins come, Holy Spirit, and with the hymns Veni Creator Spiritus and Veni Sancte Spiritus; they celebrate the Spirit's coming at Pentecost and receive the Spirit's gifts in confirmation.

o: an old title for a monastery's head gatekeeper
a Greek word for a speaker at public assemblies
one called to your side, to defend and comfort

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: Paraclete comes from a Greek courtroom word
parakletos: one called to your side, an advocate, and also a comforter.
in the Bible, spirit and breath are unrelated words
in Hebrew and Greek the same word means both: ruach, pneuma.
the Catechism says the Spirit is known by what he does
in Scripture, sacraments, prayer, gifts given to believers, and the saints.

games.q: it's Easter evening. the disciples are behind locked doors, afraid. the risen Jesus stands among them. what does he do?
o: breathe on them and say receive the Holy Ghost.
tell them to wait in silence for a year.
games.why: he breathes on them. the Spirit is given with breath, echoing God breathing life into the first human.

practice: Notice your breath without changing it: every breath you've ever taken was given, not made. If you pray, use a very old short prayer to the Spirit, one word on each slow breath: come, Holy Spirit.
If you don't, simply breathe, and think of someone who once sat down beside you when you were alone.

wordCard.voice: Paraclete. From the Greek for one called to your side: the advocate and comforter, the Holy Spirit Jesus promised would stay.

orig.note: Greek: one called to your side; advocate, comforter.

carryVoice: Your line: the breath of god. You're not the only one breathing in you. That's day three hundred seven.
